claim: Neutrophils in hai1a embryos invade the epidermis and are highly motile but move randomly.
source: Neutrophils in hai1a embryos invade the epidermis, are highly motile, but move randomly (Carney et al., 2007; Mathias et al., 2007; Figure 1A–E, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Carney et al., 2007; Mathias et al., 2007) and by data shown in Figure 1A-E and Video 1.

claim: In wild-type larvae, neutrophils were recruited from a great distance and tracked to the wound with high directionality.
source: In wild-type larvae, neutrophils were recruited from a great distance and tracked to the wound with high directionality.
evidence: Observation from experimental data comparing wild-type and hai1a mutant responses to wounding.

claim: Neutrophils in the hai1a mutant appeared largely apathetic to the wound and remained migrating randomly.
source: However, neutrophils in the hai1a mutant appeared largely apathetic to the wound and remained migrating randomly.
evidence: Observation from experimental data comparing wild-type and hai1a mutant responses to wounding.

claim: There was a mild increase in neutrophil speed in hai1a larvae following wounding, indicating that they retain capacity to respond to additive stimuli.
source: There was a mild increase in neutrophil speed in hai1a larvae following wounding, indicating that they retain capacity to respond to additive stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D and Video 2.

claim: The epidermis of hai1a mutants had regions of apoptosis at 24hpf, unlike WT.
source: Co-labelling of basal keratinocyte nuclei (using TP63 immunostaining), neutrophils (Tg(fli1:EGFP)y1 transgenic), and TUNEL labelling of apoptotic cells highlighted that whilst the epidermis of hai1a mutants, unlike WT, had regions of apoptosis at 24hpf (arrowhead, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and TUNEL labeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Neutrophils in hai1a mutants were not associated with apoptotic regions but rather found at nascent TUNEL-negative aggregates of basal keratinocytes.
source: neutrophils were not associated, but rather found at nascent TUNEL-negative aggregates of basal keratinocytes (arrow).
evidence: Observation from co-labeling experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Epidermal cell death does not directly contribute to inflammation in hai1a mutants.
source: We conclude that epidermal cell death does not directly contribute to inflammation
evidence: Inference from the observation that neutrophils are not associated with apoptotic regions.

claim: The effector stimulating neutrophils in hai1a mutants is as, or more, potent as that of wounds.
source: and that the effector stimulating neutrophils in hai1a mutants is as, or more, potent as that of wounds.
evidence: Inference from the observation that neutrophils in hai1a mutants move as fast as those in wounded WT and do not strongly respond to additional wounding.

claim: The ddfti251 allele has a missense mutation (c.749G>A; p.Gly250Asp) in hai1a.
source: sequencing of hai1a cDNA from both ddf alleles identified a nonsense mutation in the ddft419 allele (c.771T>G; p.Tyr257Ter) and a missense mutation of a highly conserved amino acid in the ddfti251 allele (c.749G>A; p.Gly250Asp) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: The ddft419 allele has a nonsense mutation (c.771T>G; p.Tyr257Ter) in hai1a.
source: sequencing of hai1a cDNA from both ddf alleles identified a nonsense mutation in the ddft419 allele (c.771T>G; p.Tyr257Ter) and a missense mutation of a highly conserved amino acid in the ddfti251 allele (c.749G>A; p.Gly250Asp) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: Peroxiredoxin4 (Prdx4) had a higher pI in both hai1at419 and hai1ati251 mutants at 24hpf and 48hpf, indicative of a change in oxidation state.
source: Rather than finding proteins with altered molecular weight, Peroxiredoxin4 (Prdx4) was identified as having a higher pI in both hai1at419 and hai1ati251 mutants at 24hpf and 48hpf, indicative of a change in oxidation state (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1J, K).
evidence: Supported by 2D gel proteomics data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1J, K.

claim: hai1a mutants have significantly higher levels of H2O2 in the trunk and tails at 24hpf and 48hpf.
source: Pentafluorobenzenesulfonyl fluorescein (PFBSF) staining Maeda et al., 2004 demonstrated significantly higher levels of H2O2 in the trunk and tails of hai1a mutants at 24hpf and 48hpf (Figure 1H–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1L, M).
evidence: Supported by PFBSF staining data shown in Figure 1H–J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L, M.

claim: The increase in H2O2 in hai1a was observed as early as 16hpf, preceding presentation of hai1a phenotypes.
source: This increase in H2O2 in hai1a was observed as early as 16hpf, and thus preceded presentation of hai1a phenotypes (Figure 1K, L).
evidence: Supported by PFBSF staining data shown in Figure 1K, L.

claim: Zygotic st14a mutants showed no overt phenotype.
source: Zygotic st14a mutants showed no overt phenotype
evidence: Observation from experimental data on st14a mutants.

claim: Maternal zygotic st14a mutants lacked ear otoliths.
source: however, maternal zygotic mutants lacked ear otoliths (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: Embryos lacking otoliths (st14asq10; hai1ahi2217 double mutants) never displayed the hai1a epidermal and neutrophil phenotypes.
source: As expected, when crossed into the hai1a background, embryos lacking otoliths (st14asq10; hai1ahi2217 double mutants) never displayed the hai1a epidermal and neutrophil phenotypes (Figure 2D–F; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D–F and Table 1.

claim: st14asq10; hai1ahi2217 double mutants had significantly reduced H2O2 levels.
source: Double mutants also had significantly reduced H2O2 levels (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by PFBSF staining data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A morpholino directed against duox successfully reduced H2O2 levels in hai1a mutants.
source: A morpholino directed against duox successfully reduced H2O2 levels (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by PFBSF staining data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Duox morpholino reduced neutrophil inflammation in hai1a mutants but did not rescue the epithelial defects.
source: A morpholino directed against duox successfully reduced H2O2 levels (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and neutrophil inflammation in hai1a mutants but did not rescue the epithelial defects (Figure 2F, G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F, G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Treatment with diphenyleneiodonium (DPI) resulted in amelioration of neutrophil inflammation, but not epithelial aggregates, in hai1a mutants.
source: Treatment with a known Duox inhibitor, diphenyleneiodonium (DPI), also resulted in amelioration of neutrophil inflammation, but not epithelial aggregates, in hai1a mutants (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Matriptase1 activity leads to excess H2O2 in hai1a mutants, which partially accounts for the neutrophil inflammation, but not epidermal defects.
source: We conclude that Matriptase1 activity leads to excess H2O2 in hai1a mutants, which partially accounts for the neutrophil inflammation, but not epidermal defects.
evidence: Inference from genetic and pharmacological experiments showing that reducing H2O2 rescues inflammation but not epithelial defects.

claim: hai1a mutants had significantly more calcium flashes in both the trunk and tail at 24hpf.
source: Timelapse imaging at 24hpf indicated that hai1a mutants had significantly more calcium flashes in both the trunk and tail (Figure 3A, B, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, Video 3).
evidence: Supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 3A, B, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, and Video 3.

claim: Increased intracellular calcium dynamics was observable as early as 16hpf, concomitant with increased H2O2, but prior to onset of hai1a phenotypes.
source: Increased intracellular calcium dynamics was observable as early as 16hpf, concomitant with increased H2O2, but prior to onset of hai1a phenotypes (Figure 3G, H, Video 4).
evidence: Supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 3G, H and Video 4.

claim: The frequency and number of calcium flashes in the trunk and tail of hai1a mutants are reduced by treatment with the IP3R inhibitor, 2-APB.
source: The frequency and number of calcium flashes in the trunk and tail of hai1a mutants are reduced by treatment with the IP3R inhibitor, 2-APB compared to control (Figure 3C, D, F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D, Video 5).
evidence: Supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 3C, D, F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D, and Video 5.

claim: Reducing calcium flashes in hai1a mutant embryos with 2-APB significantly reduced H2O2 levels.
source: Reducing calcium flashes in hai1a mutant embryos with 2-APB also significantly reduced H2O2 levels (Figure 3I, J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Supported by PFBSF staining data shown in Figure 3I, J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: 2-APB treatment partially reduced inflammation in hai1a mutants but did not rescue the epidermal defects.
source: Reducing calcium flashes in hai1a mutant embryos with 2-APB also significantly reduced H2O2 levels (Figure 3I, J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and partially reduced inflammation; however, the epidermal defects were not noticeably rescued (imaged by DIC (Differential Interference Contrast) or labelled with the TP63 antibody) (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3I–K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Thapsigargin treatment reduced neutrophil inflammation but did not rescue epidermal defects in hai1a mutants.
source: We observed similar reduction in neutrophil inflammation, but not rescue of epidermal defects, in hai1a mutants treated with thapsigargin, which inhibits the replenishment of ER calcium stores by SERCA (Figure 3K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: In hai1a mutants, IP3R-dependent calcium flashes activate Duox, flooding the epidermis with H2O2 and leading to inflammation.
source: This suggests, in hai1a mutants, that IP3R-dependent calcium flashes activate Duox, flooding the epidermis with H2O2 and leading to inflammation.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing that IP3R inhibition reduces calcium flashes, H2O2 levels, and inflammation.

claim: NfκB signalling was mostly restricted to neuromasts in WT embryos at 48hpf.
source: In WT embryos, NfkB signalling was mostly restricted to neuromasts at 48hpf
evidence: Observation from Tg(6xHsa.NFKB:EGFP)nc1 transgenic line imaging.

claim: In hai1a mutants, there was an increase in NfκB signalling fluorescence at 24hpf and a strong increase at 48hpf.
source: whilst in hai1a mutants we observed an increase in fluorescence at 24hpf and a strong increase at 48hpf.
evidence: Observation from Tg(6xHsa.NFKB:EGFP)nc1 transgenic line imaging.

claim: NfκB signalling fluorescence at both 24hpf and 48hpf was noted in epidermal aggregates and fin folds, locations of strong inflammation.
source: Fluorescence at both timepoints was noted in epidermal aggregates and fin folds, locations of strong inflammation (Figure 4A, B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The increase in NfκB signalling in 48hpf hai1a mutant embryos was confirmed by qRT-PCR of the NfκB target gene, nfkbiaa.
source: This increase in signalling in 48hpf hai1a mutant embryos was confirmed by qRT-PCR of the NfkB target gene, nfkbiaa (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: NfκB signalling is not present at early stages prior to phenotype in hai1a mutants.
source: Unlike calcium and H2O2, NfkB signalling is not present at early stages prior to phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Crossing ikbkgsq304 mutant to hai1ahi2217 resulted in a very strong rescue of neutrophil inflammation at 48hpf, but no improvement of hai1a epidermal defects.
source: Crossing this mutant to hai1ahi2217 on the Tg(mpx:eGFP)i114 background realised a very strong rescue of neutrophil inflammation at 48hpf, but no improvement of hai1a epidermal defects (Figure 4D–I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4D–I.

claim: Injection of hai1ahi2217; Tg(6xHsa.NFKB:EGFP)nc1 embryos with duox MO resulted in a strong reduction in NfκB pathway activation.
source: To demonstrate that this increase in NfkB signalling was dependent on H2O2, we injected hai1ahi2217; Tg(6xHsa.NFKB:EGFP)nc1 embryos with duox MO. We noted a strong reduction in NfkB pathway activation compared to uninjected hai1ahi2217 mutant controls (Figure 4J, K).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4J, K.

claim: Genetic ablation of NfκB signalling through use of the ikbkg mutant did not reduce H2O2 levels in hai1a mutants.
source: Conversely, genetic ablation of NfkB signalling, through use of the ikbkg mutant, did not reduce H2O2 levels in hai1a mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Supported by PFBSF staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: Treatment with 2-APB resulted in only a slight reduction in NfκB signalling in hai1a mutants.
source: Similarly, we tested if reduction of calcium flashes could also reduce NfkB signalling in hai1a mutants using 2-APB but noticed only a slight reduction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, I.

claim: Upon loss of Hai1a, IP3R-mediated release of calcium activates Duox to increase H2O2, which acts upstream of NfκB pathway activation and is necessary for the inflammation phenotype.
source: We propose that upon loss of Hai1a, IP3R-mediated release of calcium activates Duox to increase H2O2. This acts upstream of NfkB pathway activation, which occurs at later stages, and is necessary for the inflammation phenotype.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing temporal and causal relationships between calcium, H2O2, and NfκB signalling.

claim: YM-254890 significantly reduced neutrophil inflammation in hai1a mutants.
source: We found that not only did this significantly reduce neutrophil inflammation (Figure 5D, F)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D, F.

claim: YM-254890 significantly rescued the epidermal defects in hai1a mutants, with a significant reduction in TP63-positive epidermal aggregates in the trunk and improved tail fin fold integrity at 48hpf.
source: but surprisingly, it also significantly rescued the epidermal defects in hai1a mutants, with a significant reduction in TP63-positive epidermal aggregates in the trunk and improved tail fin fold integrity at 48hpf (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A–E.

claim: Treating WT embryos from 15hpf to 24hpf with 125 ng/ml PMA resulted in embryos with striking similarities to strong hai1a mutants.
source: Indeed, treating WT embryos from 15hpf to 24hpf with 125 ng/ml phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA), a DAG analogue, resulted in embryos with striking similarities to strong hai1a mutants, including a thin or absent yolk sac extension, lack of head straightening, lack of lifting the head off the yolk, and multiple epidermal aggregates on the skin (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: PMA-induced aggregates were due, at least partially, to displacement of basal keratinocytes as shown by TP63 staining.
source: These aggregates were due, at least partially, to displacement of basal keratinocytes as shown by TP63 staining where the basal keratinocyte nuclei lost their uniform distribution (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: Supported by TP63 immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D, E.

claim: Treatment from 24hpf to 48hpf with 125 ng/ml PMA led to a fin defect similar to the dysmorphic hai1a mutant fin.
source: Treatment from 24hpf to 48hpf with 125 ng/ml PMA led to a fin defect similar to the dysmorphic hai1a mutant fin (Figure 6F, G).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6F, G.

claim: PMA treatment led to a less stable cell membrane topology and dynamic cell shape in basal keratinocytes, similar to hai1a mutants.
source: Whilst the DMSO-treated transgenic larvae had very stable keratinocyte membranes and shape, PMA treatment led to a less stable cell membrane topology and dynamic cell shape, similar to hai1a mutants (Figure 6H, Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: Supported by light-sheet timelapse imaging data shown in Figure 6H and Videos 7 and 8.

claim: Most PMA-treated Tg(mpx.eGFP)i114 larvae at 48hpf had more neutrophils in the epidermis than untreated controls, which were highly migratory.
source: Most PMA-treated Tg(mpx.eGFP)i114 larvae at 48hpf also had more neutrophils in the epidermis than untreated controls, which were highly migratory (Figure 6F–G, J–K′, Video 8).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6F–G, J–K′, and Video 8.

claim: H2O2 levels were significantly increased in both trunk and tail at 24hpf in PMA-treated embryos.
source: We determined H2O2 levels in PMA-treated embryos using PFBSF staining and found that it was significantly increased in both trunk and tail at 24hpf (Figure 6L–O, R).
evidence: Supported by PFBSF staining data shown in Figure 6L–O, R.

claim: Treatment of GCaMP6s RNA-injected embryos with PMA failed to show an increase in calcium flashes, as seen in hai1a.
source: In contrast, when we treated GCaMP6s RNA-injected embryos with PMA, we failed to see an increase in calcium flashes, as seen in hai1a (Figure 6P, Q, S).
evidence: Supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 6P, Q, S.

claim: Treatment of Tg(6xHsa.NFKB:EGFP)nc1 embryos with 125 ng/ml PMA resulted in a robust increase in fluorescence, indicating that PMA activates the NfκB pathway.
source: To see if the heightened H2O2 and inflammation was also correlated with increased NfkB signalling, we treated Tg(6xHsa.NFKB:EGFP)nc1 embryos with 125 ng/ml PMA. There was a robust increase in fluorescence, indicating that PMA activates the NfkB pathway (Figure 6T, U).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6T, U.

claim: PKCδ-GFP translocated to plasma and nuclear membranes in hai1a mutants, indicating increased levels of DAG.
source: Using a GFP-tagged PKCδ fusion protein (Sivak et al., 2005), we showed that in the WT embryo there was largely diffuse cytoplasmic PKCδ-GFP signal, however, it translocated to plasma and nuclear membranes in hai1a mutants, indicating increased levels of DAG (Figure 7A, B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7A, B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Treatment of hai1ahi2217 embryos with the PKC inhibitor, GFX109203, reduced the epidermal aggregates and disruption of fin morphology.
source: This is indeed relevant to the epidermal defects, as treatment of hai1ahi2217 embryos with the PKC inhibitor, GFX109203, reduced the epidermal aggregates and disruption of fin morphology as imaged by DIC or immunostaining for TP63 (Figure 7C–H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7C–H.

claim: GFX109203 treatment somewhat reduced neutrophil inflammation in the epidermis, but not to a significant degree.
source: Neutrophil inflammation in the epidermis was somewhat reduced, but not to a significant degree (Figure 7E–I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7E–I.

claim: Epithelial defects of hai1a are due to DAG generation and PKC activation.
source: Thus, these experiments strongly suggest that epithelial defects of hai1a are due to DAG generation and PKC activation.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing that PKC inhibition rescues epithelial defects and that DAG levels are increased in hai1a mutants.

claim: There was a significant and localised increase in cytoplasmic pERK immunoreactivity in the regions of epidermal aggregate formation in hai1a mutants and in PMA-treated embryos.
source: Indeed, we observed a significant and localised increase in cytoplasmic pERK immunoreactivity (phospho-p44/42 MAPK (Erk1/2) (Thr202/Tyr204)) in the regions of epidermal aggregate formation in hai1a mutants and in PMA-treated embryos, including under the yolk at 24hpf and in the fins at 24hpf and 48hpf (Figure 8A–K, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8A–K and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: There was no increase in total ERK levels in the hai1a mutant.
source: There was no increase in total ERK levels in the mutant (Figure 8—figure supplement 1M, N).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1M, N.

claim: Increased pERK was seen in both the cytoplasm and nucleus of TP63-positive cells but was only increased in the nucleus of periderm cells.
source: Increased pERK was seen in both the cytoplasm and nucleus of TP63-positive cells but was only increased in the nucleus of periderm cells (Figure 8E–E′, Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8E–E′ and Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At 16hpf, regions of the epidermis in hai1a mutant embryos have pERK staining before overt aggregation formation.
source: We found that at 16hpf regions of the epidermis have pERK staining before overt aggregation formation (Figure 8G–H)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8G–H.

claim: Nascent aggregates in hai1a mutants contain pERK staining which increases in number over time.
source: whilst nascent aggregates also contain pERK staining which increases in number over time (Figure 8—figure supplement 1G–L).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1G–L.

claim: Both U0126 and CI-1040 inhibitors showed a significant reduction in hai1a mutant epidermal aggregates under the yolk, and restoration of the overall and tail epithelial morphology.
source: Both inhibitors showed a significant reduction in hai1a mutant epidermal aggregates under the yolk, and restoration of the overall and tail epithelial morphology, with embryos showing a hai1a phenotype class significantly reduced (Figure 9A–G, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 9A–G and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: The epidermal defects of the trunk, yolk, and tail following PMA treatment were ameliorated by concomitant U0126 treatment.
source: Similarly, the epidermal defects of the trunk, yolk, and tail following PMA treatment were also ameliorated by concomitant U0126 treatment (Figure 9H, I, Figure 9—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 9H, I and Figure 9—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Initiating U0126 treatment later at 26hpf led to only a partial rescue, indicating that the epidermal phenotypes were likely due to sustained pERK activation.
source: Initiating U0126 treatment later at 26hpf led to only a partial rescue, indicating that the epidermal phenotypes were likely due to sustained pERK activation (Figure 9—figure supplement 1K–M′).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1K–M′.

claim: Treatment with U0126 did not significantly reduce neutrophil inflammation of hai1a mutants or PMA treatment.
source: Treatment with U0126 did not significantly reduce neutrophil inflammation of hai1a mutants or PMA treatment (Figure 9L–P).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 9L–P.

claim: The inflammation phenotype is not simply a consequence of the epidermal defects.
source: This suggests that the inflammation phenotype is not simply a consequence of the epidermal defects.
evidence: Inference from the observation that U0126 rescues epithelial defects but not inflammation.

claim: Dye penetration assays showed that the epithelial barrier was not globally and overtly compromised in hai1a.
source: Furthermore, dye penetration assays showed that the epithelial barrier was not globally and overtly compromised in hai1a, underscoring that inflammation is not simply a consequence of epithelial defects (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A–H).
evidence: Supported by dye penetration assay data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2A–H.

claim: While WT basal epidermal cells of the 48hpf tail showed strong β-catenin staining at the membrane, hai1a mutants and PMA-treated embryos showed a significant loss of β-catenin at the membrane and increase in the cytoplasm.
source: Whilst the WT basal epidermal cells of the 48hpf tail showed strong staining at the membrane, hai1a mutants and PMA-treated embryos showed a significant loss of β-catenin at the membrane and increase in the cytoplasm (Figure 9Q–V, Y, Z).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9Q–V, Y, Z.

claim: Treatment of hai1a mutants with U0126 restored the membrane localisation of β-catenin.
source: Treatment of hai1a mutants with U0126 restored the membrane localisation of β-catenin (Figure 9W, X, AA).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9W, X, AA.

claim: At least RSK2a (=p90RSK2a, encoded by rps6ka3a) is expressed in basal keratinocytes at 24hpf.
source: We determined that at least RSK2a (=p90RSK2a, encoded by rps6ka3a) is expressed in basal keratinocytes at 24hpf (Figure 10A, B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 10A, B.

claim: There was a substantial increase in cytoplasmic p90RSK-pT348 signal in both hai1a mutants and PMA-treated embryos.
source: We noticed a substantial increase in cytoplasmic signal in both hai1a mutants and PMA-treated embryos. Where p90RSK-pT348 signal was largely nuclear in both basal and periderm cells in WT, it was more broadly observed in hai1a mutant fins, with an increase in the cytoplasm leading to a more uniform staining (Figure 10C–D′).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10C–D′.

claim: The increase in cytoplasmic levels of p90RSK-pT348 was observable at 17hpf prior to epithelial defects.
source: This increase in cytoplasmic levels of p90RSK-pT348 was observable at 17hpf prior to epithelial defects (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: p90RSK cytoplasmic signal was lost upon U0126 and GFX109203 treatments, showing that it was pERK and PKC dependant.
source: p90RSK cytoplasmic signal was lost upon U0126 and GFX109203 treatments, showing that it was pERK and PKC dependant (Figure 10E, E′, Figure 10—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10E, E′ and Figure 10—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Increased cytoplasmic p90RSK-pT348 was observed following PMA treatment which was reduced by co-treatment with U0126.
source: Similarly, increased cytoplasmic p90RSK-pT348 was observed following PMA treatment which was reduced by co-treatment with U0126 (Figure 10F–H′).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10F–H′.

claim: The increase in cytoplasmic p90RSK-pT348 signal, and its reduction by U0126, was significant in both hai1a mutants and PMA-treated embryos.
source: The increase in cytoplasmic p90RSK-pT348 signal, and its reduction by U0126, was significant in both hai1a mutants and PMA-treated embryos (Figure 10I, J).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 10I, J.

claim: Both BI-D1870 and dimethyl fumarate were able to reduce epidermal aggregates in hai1a mutants and restore fin morphology.
source: We noted that both inhibitors were able to reduce epidermal aggregates in hai1a mutants and restore fin morphology when visualised by DIC or TP63 immunofluorescence (Figure 10K–N, Figure 10—figure supplement 1H, I, K, L).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 10K–N and Figure 10—figure supplement 1H, I, K, L.

claim: Reduction of mutant phenotype classes by RSK inhibitors was significant at both 24hpf and 48hpf.
source: Reduction of mutant phenotype classes was significant at both 24hpf and 48hpf (Figure 10—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Dimethyl fumarate treatment restored membrane localisation of E-cadherin in hai1a mutants.
source: We then assayed if RSK inhibition can reduce the aberrant cytoplasmic E-cadherin staining in hai1a mutant basal keratinocytes and observed that dimethyl fumarate treatment restored membrane localisation of E-cadherin in the mutants (Figure 10O–Q′).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10O–Q′.

claim: Phosphorylation of RSK proteins is altered in hai1a mutants, and their inhibition appears to restore E-cadherin to the membrane and reduce epidermal aggregate formation.
source: Thus, phosphorylation of RSK proteins is altered in hai1a mutants, and their inhibition appears to restore E-cadherin to the membrane and reduce epidermal aggregate formation.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing that RSK inhibition rescues E-cadherin localization and epithelial defects.

claim: Overexpression of Matriptase in the mouse epidermis leads to epidermal papillomas, ulcerative and invasive carcinomas, and inflammation.
source: Overexpression of Matriptase in the mouse epidermis leads to epidermal papillomas, ulcerative and invasive carcinomas, and inflammation (List et al., 2005; Martin and List, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (List et al., 2005; Martin and List, 2019).

claim: An increase in the Matriptase:HAI-1 ratio has been found in a range of tumours and is predictive of poor outcome.
source: Clinically, an increase in the Matriptase:HAI-1 ratio has been found in a range of tumours and is predictive of poor outcome (Martin and List, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Martin and List, 2019).

claim: Loss of mouse Hai1 leads to epidermal and intestinal barrier defects, epithelial inflammation, and failure of placental labyrinth formation, which are all due to unrestricted Matriptase activity.
source: Loss of mouse Hai1 leads to epidermal and intestinal barrier defects, epithelial inflammation, and failure of placental labyrinth formation, which are all due to unrestricted Matriptase activity (Kawaguchi et al., 2011; Nagaike et al., 2008; Szabo et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Kawaguchi et al., 2011; Nagaike et al., 2008; Szabo et al., 2007).

claim: Mutation of the zebrafish orthologue, Hai1a, results in epidermal defects, including loss of membrane E-cadherin, aberrant mesenchymal behaviour of keratinocytes, which form cell aggregations over the body and loss of fin fold integrity.
source: Mutation of the zebrafish orthologue, Hai1a, also results in epidermal defects, including loss of membrane E-cadherin, aberrant mesenchymal behaviour of keratinocytes, which form cell aggregations over the body and loss of fin fold integrity.
evidence: Description of known phenotypes of hai1a mutants.

claim: The epidermis in hai1a mutants displays sterile inflammation and is invaded by highly active neutrophils.
source: The epidermis also displays sterile inflammation and is invaded by highly active neutrophils.
evidence: Description of known phenotypes of hai1a mutants.

claim: Genetic ablation of the myeloid lineage demonstrated that the keratinocyte phenotypes are not a consequence of the inflammation.
source: Genetic ablation of the myeloid lineage demonstrated that the keratinocyte phenotypes are not a consequence of the inflammation (Carney et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Carney et al., 2007).

claim: The strong hai1afr26 allele is embryonic lethal, dying within the first week.
source: The strong hai1afr26 allele is embryonic lethal, dying within the first week
evidence: Description of known phenotypes of hai1a alleles.

claim: The more mild allele, hai1ahi2217, is semi-viable, with epithelial defects resolved through sphingosine-1-phosphate-mediated entosis and cell extrusion.
source: whilst the more mild allele, hai1ahi2217, is semi-viable, with epithelial defects resolved through sphingosine-1-phosphate-mediated entosis and cell extrusion (Armistead et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Armistead et al., 2020).

claim: All hai1a mutant phenotypes can be ameliorated by reduction of Matriptase levels.
source: All hai1a mutant phenotypes can be ameliorated by reduction of Matriptase levels (Carney et al., 2007; Mathias et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Carney et al., 2007; Mathias et al., 2007).

claim: The G-protein-coupled receptor, proteinase-activated receptor-2 (Par2), is essential for the oncogenic and inflammatory effects of uninhibited Matriptase in zebrafish and mouse.
source: The G-protein-coupled receptor, proteinase-activated receptor-2 (Par2), is essential for the oncogenic and inflammatory effects of uninhibited Matriptase in zebrafish and mouse (Sales et al., 2015; Schepis et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Sales et al., 2015; Schepis et al., 2018).

claim: Par2 is directly activated by Matriptase proteolysis and signals through a number of heterotrimeric Gα protein subunits.
source: Par2 is directly activated by Matriptase proteolysis and signals through a number of heterotrimeric Gα protein subunits.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about Par2 signaling.

claim: Early studies in keratinocytes linked Par2 activation with intracellular Ca++ mobilisation via phospholipase C, thus implicating Gq subunit as the canonical target.
source: Early studies in keratinocytes linked Par2 activation with intracellular Ca++ mobilisation via phospholipase C, thus implicating Gq subunit as the canonical target (Schechter et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Schechter et al., 1998).

claim: Alternate Gα subunits, including Gi, Gs, and G12/13, are now known to also be activated by Par2.
source: Alternate Gα subunits, including Gi, Gs, and G12/13, are now known to also be activated by Par2 (Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Zhao et al., 2014).

claim: In vitro experiments using HEK293 cells implicated both Par2 and Gi in Matriptase-mediated Nfκb pathway activation.
source: In vitro experiments using HEK293 cells implicated both Par2 and Gi in Matriptase-mediated Nfκb pathway activation (Sales et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Sales et al., 2015).

claim: Par2 can also transactivate EGFR through an unknown mechanism, and inhibition of EGFR alleviates certain basal keratinocyte phenotypes of zebrafish hai1a mutants.
source: Par2 can also transactivate EGFR through an unknown mechanism, and inhibition of EGFR alleviates certain basal keratinocyte phenotypes of zebrafish hai1a mutants (Schepis et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Schepis et al., 2018).

claim: Peroxiredoxins are hydrogen peroxide scavengers.
source: Peroxiredoxins are hydrogen peroxide scavengers
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about peroxiredoxins.

claim: H2O2 is a known activator of inflammation in larval zebrafish.
source: and its altered oxidation state suggested that hai1a has higher H2O2 levels, a known activator of inflammation in larval zebrafish (Niethammer et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Niethammer et al., 2009).

claim: Duox is the main enzyme responsible for generating H2O2 in zebrafish.
source: To determine if reduced H2O2 could account for the rescue of hai1a phenotypes by st14a mutation, we used genetic and pharmacological inhibition of the main enzyme responsible for generating H2O2 in zebrafish, Duox.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about Duox function.

claim: Calcium flashes are known to generate H2O2 in epidermal wounds in Drosophila.
source: Duox is regulated by calcium through its EF-Hand domains, and calcium flashes are known to generate H2O2 in epidermal wounds in Drosophila (Razzell et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Razzell et al., 2013).

claim: Release of calcium from intracellular stores is regulated by IP3 receptors located on the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Release of calcium from intracellular stores is regulated by IP3 receptors located on the endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about IP3 receptor function.

claim: Seminal experiments in transgenic mice overexpressing Matriptase in the epidermis and treated with a DMBA/PMA regime concluded that Matriptase and PMA activate functionally similar carcinoma promoting pathways.
source: Seminal experiments in transgenic mice overexpressing Matriptase in the epidermis and treated with a DMBA/PMA regime concluded that Matriptase and PMA activate functionally similar carcinoma promoting pathways (List et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (List et al., 2005).

claim: In the zebrafish epidermis, misexpression of activated MEK2 generated papillomas with remarkable resemblance to the epidermal aggregates in hai1a mutants.
source: In the zebrafish epidermis, misexpression of activated MEK2 generated papillomas with remarkable resemblance to the epidermal aggregates in hai1a mutants (Chou et al., 2015), and which are not overtly proliferative.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Chou et al., 2015).

claim: In astrocytes and oesophageal or breast tumour cell lines, PAR2 stimulates migration and invasiveness through MAPK/ERK, activation of which required Gq and PIP2 hydrolysis.
source: In astrocytes and oesophageal or breast tumour cell lines, PAR2 stimulates migration and invasiveness through MAPK/ERK, activation of which required Gq and PIP2 hydrolysis (Jiang et al., 2004; McCoy et al., 2010; Morris et al., 2006; Sheng et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Jiang et al., 2004; McCoy et al., 2010; Morris et al., 2006; Sheng et al., 2019).

claim: MAPK signalling has been shown to reduce E-cadherin expression at adherens junctions and promote cytoplasmic accumulation through phosphorylation of the effector, RSK.
source: MAPK signalling has been shown to reduce E-cadherin expression at adherens junctions and promote cytoplasmic accumulation through phosphorylation of the effector, RSK (Čáslavský et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Čáslavský et al., 2013).

claim: Activation of RSK2 is associated with tumour progression, promoting invasiveness and metastasis of glioblastomas and head and neck squamous cell carcinomas.
source: Like Matriptase, activation of RSK2 is associated with tumour progression, promoting invasiveness and metastasis of glioblastomas and head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (Kang et al., 2010; Sulzmaier et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Kang et al., 2010; Sulzmaier et al., 2016).

claim: Activated RSK1 promotes invasion of melanoma clinically as well as in vitro and zebrafish melanoma models.
source: Promotion of invasiveness has also been noted for activated RSK1, which promotes invasion of melanoma clinically as well as in vitro and zebrafish melanoma models (Salhi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Salhi et al., 2015).

claim: Proximity protein labelling has identified p120-catenin as a target of RSK phosphorylation.
source: Intriguingly, proximity protein labelling has identified p120-catenin as a target of RSK phosphorylation.
evidence: Statement of recent findings in the field.

claim: p120-catenin promotes cell-cell adhesion by stabilising cadherins at junctions, a function inhibited by RSK phosphorylation.
source: This catenin promotes cell-cell adhesion by stabilising cadherins at junctions, a function inhibited by RSK phosphorylation (Méant et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Méant et al., 2020).

claim: RSK2 activity promotes cell motility through other mechanisms, including inactivation of Integrins and activation of the RhoGEF, LARG.
source: More broadly, RSK2 activity promotes cell motility through other mechanisms, including inactivation of Integrins and activation of the RhoGEF, LARG (Gawecka et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Gawecka et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2018).

claim: pERK signalling, through RSK members, significantly contributes to dissolution of adherens junctions and the hai1a epidermal phenotype.
source: Thus, we propose that pERK signalling, through RSK members, significantly contributes to dissolution of adherens junctions and the hai1a epidermal phenotype.
evidence: Inference from experiments showing that RSK inhibition rescues adherens junction defects and epithelial phenotypes.

claim: MMPs, HB-EGF, EGFR, and AKT are downstream of Matriptase and PAR2 function.
source: Indeed, others have indicated MMPs, HB-EGF, EGFR, and AKT and are downstream of Matriptase and PAR2 function (List et al., 2005; Schepis et al., 2018; Darmoul et al., 2004; Chung et al., 2013; Rattenholl et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (List et al., 2005; Schepis et al., 2018; Darmoul et al., 2004; Chung et al., 2013; Rattenholl et al., 2007).

claim: Matriptase promotes HGF–cMet signalling in mouse.
source: Furthermore, Matriptase promotes HGF–cMet signalling in mouse (Szabo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Szabo et al., 2011).

claim: PI3K/AKT and MEK/ERK function in parallel downstream of PAR2.
source: A number of reports have demonstrated that PI3K/AKT and MEK/ERK function in parallel downstream of PAR2 (Sheng et al., 2019; Tanaka et al., 2008; van der Merwe et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Sheng et al., 2019; Tanaka et al., 2008; van der Merwe et al., 2009).

claim: PKC activates both MEK/ERK and EGFR independently following PAR2 stimulation.
source: Furthermore, there is evidence that PKC activates both MEK/ERK and EGFR independently following PAR2 stimulation, and that PI3K is activated by PAR2 via Gq (Wang and DeFea, 2006; Al-Ani et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Wang and DeFea, 2006; Al-Ani et al., 2010).

claim: Cell identity, subcellular localisation, β-arrestin scaffolding, and biased agonism/antagonism are known to generate alternative downstream outputs from PAR2.
source: Cell identity, subcellular localisation, β-arrestin scaffolding, and biased agonism/antagonism are known to generate alternative downstream outputs from PAR2 (Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Zhao et al., 2014).
